title: James P. Johnson as a great figure after Fats
summary: James P. Johnson came up in San Juan Hill, played anything and studied music, but was less colorful than Fats.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Now, I wondered -- you know, when -- well, I know -- I mean, I know who you thought was the greatest figure in jazz because you've told me in so many of our conversations, and that's Fats.
But if you could exclude that. He's in a category by himself. What other person comes to mind as one of the really great names in jazz?

James P. Johnson would be, because that's -- James P. -- that's got a lot of what he has, James P. But he didn't get -- he wasn't as colorful as Fats. He didn't associate the same way that Fats did. He didn't travel the same streets Fats traveled.
What was -- I've heard you describe, you know, Fats that is aside from his size, but his very energy and personality filled a room. Now, how would you -- how would you describe James P.?
Well, James P. came up way back in, I'd say, 60th Street, across 9th Avenue, down San Juan Hill, we called it. He came up from down there with -- but he was
always a terrific talent. He could play -- he could play anything that could be played, and before he studied music, and then he went to school and studied music, and then he had it made.
Sure, he got all the back --
He could do anything that he heard right here, anything.
And then he went to school, and he could also play -- from the music.
From the music, he felt, and he was just twice as good as you are.
